segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Every server in Raft is in exactly one of three states. Follower, candidate, or leader.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Followers are passive. They just respond to requests from leaders and candidates. They don't initiate anything.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: A candidate is a server that's trying to become leader. It's in the middle of running an election.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And the leader handles all client requests and replicates the log. If a client talks to a follower, the follower redirects it to the leader.

segments.speaker: interviewer

segments.text: Now the concept that ties all of this together, and I want you to really internalize this one, is the term.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Each term begins with an election. One or more candidates try to become leader. If a candidate wins, it's the leader for the rest of that term.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: If nobody wins, which can happen, it's called a split vote, then that term ends with no leader, and a new term with a new election starts shortly after.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And the guarantee is, there is at most one leader in any given term. That's election safety.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So the definition, for your notes. A term is a monotonically increasing number that acts as a logical clock. Each term has at most one leader. Some terms have no leader.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And every server stores its current term number, and it includes that term in every message it sends.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And here's the rule that's going to do a lot of work for us. If a server ever sees a message with a term bigger than its own current term, it immediately updates its term to the bigger one, and if it was a leader or a candidate, it steps down and becomes a follower.

segments.text: And if a server receives a request with a term smaller than its own, it rejects the request. Stale term, you're out of date, go away.

segments.text: Raft uses a heartbeat mechanism. The leader periodically sends empty AppendEntries messages to all followers. That's the heartbeat. It says, I'm still here, I'm still the leader.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: As long as a follower keeps receiving valid heartbeats from a current leader, it stays a follower.

segments.speaker: interviewer

segments.speaker: interviewer

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Then one of three things happens. One, it wins the election. Two, some other server establishes itself as leader. Or three, a timeout goes by with no winner.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: The leader first commits a special configuration entry that represents both configurations together, C old comma new. segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Once C old comma new is committed, the leader then commits an entry with just C new. After that commits, the old configuration is irrelevant, and servers that aren't in the new configuration can be shut down.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And at no point can the old and new configurations make independent decisions, because in the middle, you need both.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Paxos is Leslie Lamport's algorithm. The original paper is "The Part-Time Parliament". He wrote it around 1990, it was published in 1998, and it's written as an allegory about a fictional parliament on a Greek island, which did not help anyone understand it.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So in 2001 he wrote "Paxos Made Simple", which starts with, and I'm paraphrasing, "the Paxos algorithm, when presented in plain English, is very simple". People have opinions about that sentence.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Basic Paxos, sometimes called single-decree Paxos, agrees on one single value. There are proposers, acceptors, and learners.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: It runs in two phases. Phase 1, prepare and promise. A proposer picks a proposal number and asks a majority of acceptors to promise not to accept anything with a lower number, and to tell it about any value they've already accepted.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Phase 2, accept and accepted. The proposer asks the acceptors to accept a value, and it has to use the value from the highest-numbered proposal that any of them already accepted, if there was one. If a majority accepts, the value is chosen.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Notice what's doing the work there. Majorities, and the overlap between the prepare majority and any earlier accept majority. Same core idea as Raft. It's always the overlap.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: To replicate a whole log you run many instances of Paxos, one per log slot, and in practice you elect a stable leader so you can skip phase 1 most of the time. That's called Multi-Paxos.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And the problem historically was that Multi-Paxos was never fully specified in one place. Everyone who built it filled in the gaps differently. There's a well-known Google paper, "Paxos Made Live", about building Chubby, where they basically say the gap between the paper and a real system is enormous.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So how does Raft relate? The honest answer is, Raft is very close to a particular, well-specified flavor of Multi-Paxos with a strong leader.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: The main differences. One, in Raft, the log has no holes. Entries are committed in order, and a follower's log is always a prefix-matching copy of the leader's. In Multi-Paxos, different slots can be decided independently and out of order, so you can have gaps.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Two, Raft's election restriction means a new leader already has all committed entries, so log entries only flow from leader to followers. In many Paxos variants a new leader has to learn missing entries from other servers during its first phase.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Three, Raft bundles leader election, log management, and membership into one specification with a reference to exactly which state is persistent. That completeness is honestly the biggest practical difference.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: What's not different. Fault tolerance. Both need 2f plus 1 servers to tolerate f crash failures. Both are safe under asynchrony and live only under partial synchrony. Neither handles malicious servers. Performance in the normal case is basically the same, one round of messages to a majority per command.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So is Raft strictly better then? Like, why would anyone still use Paxos?

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Not strictly better. Raft's strong leader is also a bottleneck, every write goes through one machine. There are leaderless or multi-leader variants in the Paxos family, like EPaxos, that can do better for geo-distributed workloads with low conflict rates. And a lot of existing systems are built on Paxos and work fine.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Raft's win is that you can teach it in 90 minutes and a team can implement it correctly. That matters a lot. But "easier to understand" is not the same as "faster" or "more available". Keep those separate.

The Jepsen analyses by Kyle Kingsbury have found real consistency bugs in systems that use Raft or Paxos, and the bug is almost always in the stuff around the algorithm, not in the algorithm.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: The problem. The log grows forever. Every command ever issued is in there. That takes more and more disk space, and when a server restarts, replaying millions of entries to rebuild the state machine takes forever.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: The simplest fix is snapshotting. Each server, independently, takes a snapshot of its current state machine state, writes it to stable storage, and then throws away all the log entries up through the last entry included in that snapshot.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Note, independently. Servers don't coordinate their snapshots. Each server snapshots its own committed state whenever it wants, usually when the log hits some size threshold. Only committed, applied entries can go into a snapshot.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And the snapshot has to include a little metadata. The last included index, which is the index of the last entry the snapshot replaces. And the last included term, the term of that entry.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Why do we need those two? Because of the AppendEntries consistency check. The first entry after the snapshot needs a prevLogIndex and prevLogTerm to check against, and those entries are gone. So the snapshot remembers them.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And the snapshot also includes the latest configuration, for membership changes.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Now, a complication. Sometimes the leader has already discarded the entries it needs to send to a slow follower. Like a follower that's been down for an hour, or a brand new server.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Then the leader sends its snapshot instead, using the third RPC, InstallSnapshot. When the follower gets it, if the snapshot covers everything in its log, it discards its whole log and replaces its state with the snapshot. If the snapshot only covers a prefix of its log, it deletes that prefix and keeps the entries after it.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And that's a slight departure from the strong leader principle, since followers can snapshot on their own. But the data still only flows from the leader. Followers just reorganize what they already have.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Practically, the tricky part is that writing a snapshot of a big state machine takes time, and you don't want to stop serving requests while you do it. A common trick is copy-on-write, like forking the process on Linux so the child writes the snapshot while the parent keeps going.
